  • The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.
  • In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba's social media posts have previously sparked diplomatic tensions.

The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.

In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns.

The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.

The Ugandan government has yet to respond.

The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours.

Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.

Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.

Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever.

The Ugandan general who lobs grenades on Twitter.

In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahima ethnic community.

The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province.

They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.

He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.

Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.

Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.

It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.

During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed.".

The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels, with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.

Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo.

"These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.

"The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future".

The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".

It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.

In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.

In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.

The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.

In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The flooded mine is in Bogor in West Java.

It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground.

According to recent reports, rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. On Monday night, he and at least 25 other miners were digging in an open-pit mine about 100m (328ft) deep, when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood the two shafts.

Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site. At least 13 more are thought to still be missing.

Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with personnel using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow and slippery mine shafts, which are continually being flooded from below.

Above ground, ambulances and medical personnel are ready and waiting to transport victims.

"We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, noted in a statement on Wednesday.

"The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely.".

Rescuers have been working day and night to find survivors in the flooded mine shaft.

Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but remains widespread in rural parts of the mineral-rich archipelago.

Multiple studies show that over the past ten years the illegal industry has rapidly flourished, often in correlation with rising gold prices. In early 2026, those prices reached an all-time high â spurring a gold rush that prompted mine operators across the country to expand their operations.

This included state-owned mining tech giant Aneka Tambang (Antam), which owns the business permit for the area in which this week's flooded mine is located. Antam have said the mine was not theirs and was operating without their authorisation.

On Wednesday, while rescue operations there were underway, West Java Regional Police separately declared that they had uncovered 24 cases of illegal mining across the province between October and November alone.

But Bisman Bakhtiar, Executive Director of the Center for Energy and Mining Law Studies, told the BBC earlier this year that the actual number of illegal mines in Indonesia is higher than the government's figures.

"[The government figures are] what's been recorded. That means there must be more than that," he mentioned, noting that law enforcement operations have had little impact on the sector.

"It's still very massive and very major because this has been going on for a very long time.".

Others allege that the illegal industry is underpinned by corruption.

Laode M Syarif, former deputy chairman of the Corruption Eradication Committee, mentioned that unofficial mining is difficult to eradicate because every illegal mine has "backing", usually from "police and military or high-ranking officials in local and provincial governments".

"As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue," he said.

In many cases, though, the allure of these mines is simple: they offer an economic lifeline to people with few other viable prospects.

Despite the value of gold having dipped in recent months, countless illegal miners throughout Indonesia are still eagerly digging for paydirt.

But the lack of regulation and poor construction in the pits also means accidents are relatively common â whether from landslides, floods, or exposure to hazardous gases, all of which have claimed lives in recent years.

Relatives of the missing Bogor miners have been waiting near the site for news of their loved ones.

Earlier this year, in the same area as this week's flooded mine, 11 illegal gold miners reportedly died after a carbon monoxide leak inside a shaft.

Elsewhere, in West Sumatra, nine people were killed at an illegal gold mine in May after heavy rain triggered the collapse of a 30-metre cliff, burying 12 miners in total.

Industry observers note that there are numerous reports of other such incidents across the Indonesian archipelago. But the illegal nature of the small-scale gold mining sector obfuscates the true number of casualties.

Even this week, when asked how many miners were in the pits in Bogor when they flooded, M Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency, mentioned the total casualty figure "is still unclear".

Recent findings suggest that "Some say 20 people, others say 29 people," Hamdani told Indonesian news outlet Detik. "The problem is that no one reported it and no one wants to report it.".

The Indonesian Ombudsman on Thursday urged law enforcement officials to conduct a thorough investigation of the incident and to address the larger systemic concern behind it.

"This should be a momentum for all parties to resolve the [illegal gold mining] problem comprehensively, not just taking action after the incident or closing the holes discovered," said Abdul Ghoffar, a member of the Indonesian Ombudsman.

"We need to uncover the entire [illegal gold mining] chain," he continued. "We must not allow only the miners in the field to be seen and prosecuted, while those who control the activities, provide capital and facilities, store, and market the mined products remain untouched.

"Law enforcement must target the actors and networks that keep this illegal activity going.".

Recent findings suggest that as rescue operations continue and more bodies are recovered, the picture is becoming less murky. But even if there are survivors among those who remain missing, time may be running out.

More than three days since the shafts flooded, the relatives of the anonymous men in the mines are desperately waiting to hear whether their loved ones survived.

As she waits for news of her father, Rani indicates: "I hope he's found soon.".

A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.

Khaled Abu Nada and his wife Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada were killed in the air strike.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.

The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.

  • Three of them are in critical condition, according to news agency AFP, which said the local hospital had revised its earlier assessment of four.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: Fire and smoke billows out of refinery owned by energy manufacturer Bangchak Corporation.

Nine people have been injured after an explosion at an oil refinery in Bangkok, authorities have remarked.

Three of them are in critical condition, according to news agency AFP, which said the local hospital had revised its earlier assessment of four.

A fire broke out after the blast at the Phra Khanong facility run by energy giant Bangchak Corporation in the east of Thailand's capital at around 14:45 (07:45 GMT).

The firm said the fire was brought under control and put out within 30 minutes, adding that the cause of the incident was being investigated.

Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as local officials told residents to leave the area.

An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.

Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.

On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.

He stated the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.

Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.

According to recent reports, it confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The manufacturer has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.

An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

Breaking: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1104 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Co)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's music.
  • Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.
  • Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's music.

Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.

Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.

Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".

Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran stated in a statement on Wednesday.

Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off.

He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.

Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates remarked: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.".

They mentioned their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.

Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart".

"Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later.".

Watch: Andy Taylor tells the BBC about his cancer diagnosis in 2023.

Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".

Kemp stated Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix.".

In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".

US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".

Belinda Carlisle mentioned she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You.

Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".

Taylor (second left) married his wife Tracey at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Los Angeles in 1982.

Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together.".

She said he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".

Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songs.

The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.

He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.

The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.

Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.

Duran Duran bridged the sounds of pop, funk, disco, punk and newly introduced wave with a sound that remains indelibly tied to the 1980s.

Duran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs.

Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly introduced MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.

They became so popular in the US that the press labeled them the leaders of a "second British invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.

During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station.

The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.

"We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.

"We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral.".

He went on to play on Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.

Taylor quit Duran Duran at the height of their fame in 1985, but rejoined the band several times in the 2000s and contributed to their most recent album, Danse Macabre.

After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.

In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.

When the group took the stage, Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.

Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.

The following BBC programmes will pay tribute to Taylor:.

Duran Duran at the BBC, on BBC Four on Friday 27 November at 21:30 GMT.

Sounds of the 80s, on Radio 2 on Saturday 28 November at at 18:00 GMT.

    Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (489 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Co)
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Myanmar's president Min Aung Hlaing has led the country since he seized power in a 2021 military coup.
    • Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has remarked in his first public comments since the court decision.
    • The ICJ's landmark ruling last week found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Myanmar's president Min Aung Hlaing has led the country since he seized power in a 2021 military coup.

    Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has remarked in his first public comments since the court decision.

    The ICJ's landmark ruling last week found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee.

    Myanmar denied committing genocide, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups. It is the first state to have been found in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

    Min Aung Hlaing noted "the term 'genocide' had seriously affected the country's reputation", state media report.

    "Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate," the country's coup leader-turned-president said at a meeting on Wednesday, according to state media.

    The statement did not specify which parts of the ruling the country objects to.

    The genocide case, brought by The Gambia in 2019, centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

    Industry observers note that the ICJ determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed during the operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.

    The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world.

    The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

    The ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

    The ICJ ordered Myanmar to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure should be determined at a later date.

    The court also ordered Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and immediately investigate those suspected of breaking the Convention.

    But the ICJ does not have the power to enforce these demands. Instead it has to rely on the UN Security Council and political pressure to make its rulings stick.

    While the ruling was largely symbolic, it was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups who have long called attention to the suffering faced by the Rohingya.

    More than a dozen countries have acknowledged the ICJ ruling, and the UK has revealed sanctions on several senior Myanmar military leaders.

    Sources indicate that myanmar has been devastated by civil war since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup to oust civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021. The move turned Myanmar into an international pariah, and its military regime has faced sweeping international sanctions.

    Since then, Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to reintegrate Myanmar into the international community, but it remains largely shut out of key diplomatic arenas.

    Hope for millions as cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (622 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Co)
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lenacapavir has received WHO's approval for HIV prevention.
    • Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.
    • The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lenacapavir has received WHO's approval for HIV prevention.

    Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.

    The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.

    The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (Â£30) per person annually.

    Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.

    The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.

    The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.

    Focus on Africa podcast: Lenacapavir offering upcoming hope for HIV prevention?

    Landmark deal paves way for cheaper HIV protection jab.

    Lenacapavir works by targeting the protective protein shell of HIV, disrupting the virus's ability to multiply and establish an infection in the body.

    In a landmark clinical trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa in 2024, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV.

    Health experts say the injection offers a major advantage over existing HIV prevention pills, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which must be taken every day and can carry social stigma.

    The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the drug for HIV prevention in July 2025.

    The Global Fund described the arrival of the drug in Africa as a "major breakthrough" in the fight against HIV, saying cheaper supplies would help reach millions more people at risk of infection.

    "These deliveries mark an unprecedented acceleration and expansion in access to a highly effective, quality-assured generic HIV prevention medicine in low- and middle-income settings," the group said in a statement on Wednesday.

    More than 189,000 people across 10 countries have already received their first injection of lenacapavir, according to the Global Fund.

    The organisation expects 24 countries to have received supplies by the end of this year and, working with the US government, prepares to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.

    It is eventually expected to be available in 120 low- and middle-income countries.

    Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV globally, with adolescent girls and young women disproportionately affected.

    Recent findings suggest that south Africa has the world's largest HIV-positive population, with nearly eight million people living with the virus. It is among the countries expected to receive the cheaper injection.

    Some 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV last year, while 570,000 died from HIV-related illnesses, according to the WHO.

    The rollout comes amid concerns that sweeping cuts to US foreign aid under President Donald Trump's administration could undermine decades of progress in tackling HIV in Africa, where many countries rely heavily on international funding for prevention and treatment.

    The UN aims to end Aids as a public health threat by 2030.

    • Sources close to the investigation were earlier quoted by state media as saying a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the fuel truck, causing the driver to lose control.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Egyptian authorities have arrested a man accused of causing a tanker crash and massive fire that killed 31 people on a busy Cairo highway.

    The public prosecutor's office said the motorist had confessed to driving at 110km/h (68mph) along a section of ring road, to the north of the old city centre, and clipping the tanker with the side of his car as he changed lanes.

    Sources close to the investigation were earlier quoted by state media as saying a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the fuel truck, causing the driver to lose control.

    Twenty-one others were injured in the crash in the Warraq neighbourhood on Wednesday evening, with hospitals treating patients for burns and smoke inhalation.

    The public prosecutor's office stated on Thursday that "upon questioning the suspect and confronting him with the findings of the investigation... he confessed to committing the act".

    According to recent reports, "He added that, while moving between traffic lanes and overtaking vehicles, the left side of his car collided with the right rear side of the tanker. This caused him to lose control of the steering wheel and his car veered to the far right of the road.".

    At the same time, one of the fuel tanker's tyres burst, causing it to veer into the highway's central reservation, hit the concrete barrier and overturn, spilling fuel and igniting a fire, the prosecutor's office said.

    Egyptian authorities have not named the suspect accused of causing the fatal crash, but they said he had been travelling with his father at the time.

    The raised motorway - a major artery for traffic around the Egyptian capital - was reopened by emergency services hours after the crash occurred, with the burnt-out wrecks of cars shifted to the side by bulldozers and diggers.

    A cabinet minister stated on Thursday that 10 million Egyptian pounds (Â£139,000; $182,000) had been donated to the families of the victims, while the nation's sports minister said all state-run celebratory activities would be cancelled in the aftermath of the crash.

    In a recent development, egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years. Road collisions are also common, attributed to poor maintenance and violations of traffic laws, and leading to thousands of road deaths a year.

    Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway.

    • Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.
    • The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing tech giant Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry noted.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A Rheinmetall facility in Kuwait was targeted by Iran, Italian and Kuwaiti authorities said.

    Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.

    The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing tech giant Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry noted.

    Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the incident looked "suspicious" and that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the cause".

    Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.

    It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.

    Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.

    The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.

    On Thursday, Araghchi said he had expressed condolences over the deaths in calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and that the incident looked like a "precooked recipe for war", without expanding further.

    Earlier, the country's armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi remarked "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by Iran.

    Kuwait's Army mentioned the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.

    Italy's foreign minister was quoted by Italian media as saying that investigations demonstrated that the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran and that Iranian proxies were known to carry out attacks in the region.

    "The Rheinmetall Group is in deep mourning," the German firm said in a statement confirming the deaths of two of its staff members.

    "Two highly valued employees lost their lives while carrying out their professional duties, as they were providing technical support for air defence systems," it added.

    "Protecting people in the country was a matter of profound importance to them.

    "Company management and the workforce are devastated that our colleagues have now lost their lives.".

    Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.

    The men had been performing maintenance on systems used by the Kuwait Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa citing Italy's foreign ministry.

    Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.

    "My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families.".

    European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf.

    "Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security matter for us all.".

    A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of Fresh Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has remarked.

    Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.

    The Upcoming Mexico Corrections Department noted that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.

    She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.

    Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.

    The corrections department has remarked that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an patch.

    Industry observers note that the Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is right now in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach noted.

    "It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.

    All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.

    However the prison where she was being held, the Western Upcoming Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are right now allowed.

    The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

    • An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have stated.
    • The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Med Emre vessel capsized near Ibiza and Spain's Clara Campoamor, a pollution control vessel, was sent to assess the environmental impact.

    An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have stated.

    The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.

    The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.

    The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.

    "There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.

    Elena Delgado, maritime captain of Valencia, told news agency AFP that a small slick that had formed around the boat had "disappeared".

    "The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out on Friday morning.

    Earlier, regional emergencies director Pablo GÃ¡rriz stated the tanker had not completely sunk, as had originally been reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.

    The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.

    The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.

    Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew noted it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.

    The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens stated.

    Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

    In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline. It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

    She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer stated Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.

    But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).

    In a recent development, last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.

    He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).

    Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.

    Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.

    Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".

    The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.

    Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation.".

    Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".

    French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.

    #25. German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1372 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

    German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Co)
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin Reuter.
    • A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.
    • Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin Reuter.

    A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

    Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.

    The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

    His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.

    In a recent development, we confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

    Recent findings suggest that reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

    It has been revealed that the BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper SÃ¼ddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.

    Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.

    Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.

    A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled).

    At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.

    There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.

    In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

    It has been revealed that there was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that.".

    It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.

    French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German manufacturer is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.

    The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.

    While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".

    Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.

    In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.

    In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.

    Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.

    News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.

    Recent findings suggest that he was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.

    One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cans.

    The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

    The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.

    Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.

    The men claimed they had been paid up to â¬1,000-a-time (Â£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.

    It has been revealed that "Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is noted to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye.".

    Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boats.

    Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.

    Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.

    Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.

    Industry observers note that on the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.

    The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.

    Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German police.

    Meanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.

    Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.

    The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.

    It has been revealed that we confronted Marvin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rules.

    When we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.

    Sources indicate that he then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.

    We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.

    It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.

    Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near Dortmund.

    In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.

    The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the latest law had been used.

    Industry observers note that small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

    The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an key piece of the puzzle".

    While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.

    The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

    Breaking: New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If the ruling bloc cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.
    • New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.
    • In a recent development, it now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If the ruling bloc cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.

    New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.

    In a recent development, it now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.

    The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.

    A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.

    Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.

    "Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.

    It has been revealed that labour leader Chris Hipkins stated his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More Fresh Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said.

    In a recent development, new Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes â one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative.

    Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests, picked up five.

    Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.

    "There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.

    Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.

    But today's official tally highlights it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.

    Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.

    Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.

    In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.

    "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," mentioned 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.

    A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.

    More than half of the country no longer see Newly introduced Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.

    Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden, moving to Australia.
